name: AI Agents and the MCP Ecosystem
blurb: Autonomous and multi-agent systems, planning and memory, tool use, and the Model Context Protocol servers, clients, registries, and security model.

built.name: Autonomous Agents
built.detail: This section covers single agents that take a goal and run their own loop of planning, tool calls, and self-correction without a person approving each step.

built.name: Multi-agent Systems
built.detail: This section covers what happens when more than one agent is involved: orchestration frameworks that run a set of agents, delegation patterns that hand work between them, and the wire protocols agents from different vendors use to talk to each other.

built.name: Agent Memory and Planning
built.detail: This section covers the layer that lets an agent carry state across turns and across sessions: storing what happened, retrieving the relevant part of it later, and building the working context an agent plans against.

built.name: Coding and Browser Agents
built.detail: This section covers agents that operate a real tool rather than only producing text: agents that read and edit a codebase and run its tests, and agents that drive a browser by clicking, typing, and reading pages.

built.name: Voice and Service Agents
built.detail: This section covers agents that hold a spoken conversation in real time: the frameworks that stitch together speech recognition, a model, speech synthesis, and a telephony or WebRTC transport tight enough that a caller does not hear the seams.

built.name: MCP Servers
built.detail: Every active server in the official Model Context Protocol registry: who publishes it, what it exposes, whether it is hosted or runs locally, and where to get it.

built.name: MCP SDKs and Registries
built.detail: The tooling and directories around the protocol.

built.name: MCP Security and Authentication
built.detail: Trust boundaries, credentials, and the failure modes.

built.name: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol
built.detail: The open standard for agent-to-agent delegation: Agent Cards, task lifecycle, three protocol bindings, enterprise auth schemes, and how it complements MCP. Google-originated, Linux Foundation-governed, verified from the v1.0 specification.

title: AI Agents and the MCP Ecosystem
answer: Autonomous and multi-agent systems, planning and memory, tool use, and the Model Context Protocol servers, clients, registries, and security model.

reading.body:
The MCP server registry holds 2,580 active entries, more than two orders of magnitude above every other category in this map.

That gap is the useful fact. MCP clients number 8, SDKs and registries 8, and the agent categories range from 3 to 5. A protocol with thousands of servers and a handful of clients is a supply-side ecosystem: the tooling to expose capabilities has outrun the applications that consume them. For AI specifically, MCP servers are the layer that lets a model reach files, databases, and internal systems, so the count is a rough measure of how much of the world has been made addressable to agents. It is not a measure of how much of it is used.

The rest of the map is thin by comparison and should be read as a taxonomy rather than a census. Autonomous agents, multi-agent systems, memory and planning, coding and browser agents, and voice agents are each described as categories with counts in the single digits. A2A and MCP security carry no count at all. The data does not say how these categories relate in deployment, how many agents run in production, or what compute any of it consumes.

Nothing here speaks to buildings or power. The binding constraint this page can show is not physical. It is that capability has been published faster than it has been adopted.
